nodes.label: Genghis Khan invades Khwarazmia
nodes.full: Genghis Khan's response to the Khwarazm-Shah's murder of a Mongol trade mission was a campaign of conquest so thorough that it effectively ended organised Khwarazmian resistance within two years — the opening catastrophe from which the Iranian plateau's political and demographic landscape would not fully recover for generations.
nodes.src: Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay (History of the World Conqueror), the fullest contemporary Persian account of the invasion.

nodes.label: Sack of Merv, Nishapur, Herat
nodes.full: Mongol forces destroyed Merv, Nishapur and Herat in successive campaigns, contemporary chroniclers describing death tolls in the hundreds of thousands per city — figures modern historians treat as likely exaggerated by the sources' own conventions but that nonetheless point to genuinely unprecedented urban destruction and depopulation across Khorasan.
nodes.src: Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay, on the sack of Merv and Nishapur, with the customary caution that medieval casualty figures require critical treatment.

nodes.label: Conquest toll disputed
nodes.full: Persian chroniclers writing within living memory of the conquest recorded casualty figures for cities like Merv and Nishapur that would, if taken literally, exceed those cities' entire plausible populations — modern historians read these numbers as a genuine, deliberately amplified expression of trauma and loss rather than a reliable body count, without doubting that the underlying devastation was real and historically unprecedented in scale.
nodes.src: Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; modern demographic critique of medieval casualty figures for the Mongol conquest of Khorasan.

nodes.label: Qanat recovery
nodes.full: Many qanat systems fell into disrepair or were deliberately destroyed during the initial Mongol conquest, and Ghazan's later land reforms specifically targeted their restoration as a precondition for reviving abandoned agricultural land — infrastructure recovery treated as inseparable from the fiscal and political reforms it was meant to support.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on Ghazan's agricultural restoration measures.

nodes.label: Jalal al-Din and the interregnum
nodes.full: The last Khwarazm-Shah's son Jalal al-Din Mingburnu fought a remarkable multi-year rearguard campaign against Mongol forces before his final defeat, after which Iran passed through three decades of indirect Mongol overlordship — governed by local rulers and Mongol-appointed commanders answering to the distant Great Khan — before Hulagu's arrival formalised direct Ilkhanid rule.
nodes.src: al-Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din Mankubirti, on Jalal al-Din's campaigns.

nodes.label: Battle of Parwan
nodes.full: Jalal al-Din inflicted a rare and notable defeat on a Mongol detachment at Parwan — one of the few clear Khwarazmian victories of the entire war — before being decisively beaten himself soon after at the Indus, a reminder that Mongol forces, while overwhelmingly dominant, were not literally unbeatable in the field.
nodes.src: al-Nasawi, Sirat al-Sultan Jalal al-Din Mankubirti, on the Battle of Parwan.

nodes.label: Hulagu founds the Ilkhanate
nodes.full: Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu destroyed the Nizari Ismaili state at Alamut and the Abbasid Caliphate at Baghdad within two years of each other, then established an independent Mongol khanate over Iran and Iraq based at Maragheh — nominally subordinate to the Great Khan in China but in practice a fully autonomous state from its founding.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on Hulagu's campaigns and the founding of the Ilkhanate.

nodes.label: Alamut destroyed
nodes.full: Hulagu's forces captured and dismantled the Nizari Ismaili fortress network at Alamut, ending a century and a half of independent Nizari statehood within Iran and destroying the movement's library and archives — a far more total and permanent end than the Seljuks, for all their efforts, had ever achieved against the Assassins.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh; Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay, on the fall of Alamut.

nodes.label: Sack of Baghdad
nodes.full: Hulagu's army, launched from his Iranian base, besieged and sacked Baghdad and executed the last Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim — ending five centuries of Abbasid caliphal authority in a campaign whose logistics and command were centred entirely in Ilkhanid Iran, even though the devastation fell on Iraq.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on the fall of Baghdad.

nodes.label: Ayn Jalut
nodes.full: A Mamluk army decisively defeated a Mongol force at Ayn Jalut in Palestine, the first major battlefield defeat of a Mongol army anywhere and the point beyond which Mongol westward expansion never again advanced — a strategic ceiling the Ilkhanate spent the rest of its history trying, and failing, to break through.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir's continuators and Mamluk-era Arabic chronicles, on the Battle of Ayn Jalut.

nodes.label: Maragheh Observatory
nodes.full: Hulagu funded Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's observatory at Maragheh, equipped with the era's most sophisticated astronomical instruments and a major library, where Tusi developed the mathematical 'Tusi couple' device for modelling planetary motion without Ptolemy's problematic equant — a solution historians of science have traced through later Islamic astronomy into Copernicus's own work three centuries later.
nodes.src: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, Zij-i Ilkhani (the astronomical tables produced at Maragheh).

nodes.label: Maragheh instruments
nodes.full: The Maragheh Observatory housed large-scale mural instruments, armillary spheres and a substantial library reportedly including texts acquired from as far as China — instrumentation and resources on a scale that let its astronomers achieve measurably more accurate planetary observations than most of their contemporaries anywhere in the world.
nodes.src: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's own description of the observatory's instruments and library.

nodes.label: Before the conversion
nodes.full: Three decades of Ilkhans ruled a religiously pluralist court — shamanist and Buddhist by inherited Mongol custom, with influential Nestorian Christian and Muslim factions alike — while fighting recurring wars against the rival Mamluk Sultanate and the Golden Horde and periodically exploring alliance with Christian Europe against their common Mamluk enemy.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on the reigns of Abaqa, Tekuder, Arghun, Gaykhatu and Baydu.

nodes.label: Yassa beside Islamic law
nodes.full: Before Ghazan's conversion, the Ilkhanate governed through a genuine legal pluralism — the Mongol customary law code (Yassa) attributed to Genghis Khan operating alongside Islamic sharia, local Persian administrative custom, and separate legal provisions for Christian and other subject communities, each applied depending on who was involved in a given case.
nodes.src: Comparative legal-historical analysis of Ilkhanid-era legal pluralism prior to Ghazan's Islamisation of the state.

nodes.label: Pluralist court
nodes.full: The pre-conversion Ilkhanid court patronised Buddhist temples, inherited Mongol shamanist practice, and gave real influence to Nestorian Christians — Hulagu's own principal wife Doquz Khatun was an outspoken Christian whose advocacy reportedly helped spare Baghdad's Christian community during the 1258 sack — before Ghazan's conversion narrowed this pluralism decisively toward Islam.
nodes.src: Bar Hebraeus, Chronicon, a Christian source describing Doquz Khatun's religious influence at court.

nodes.label: Bar Sauma’s embassy
nodes.full: A Nestorian Christian monk born in Mongol-ruled China, Rabban Bar Sauma travelled west as the Ilkhan Arghun's ambassador, meeting the kings of France and England, the Byzantine emperor and the Pope in Rome to propose a joint Christian-Mongol alliance against the Mamluks — a reverse Marco Polo journey, from the Mongol world toward Europe, that never achieved its diplomatic goal but produced an extraordinary firsthand travel account.
nodes.src: The History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sauma (Syriac, anonymous), the sole surviving account of the embassy.

nodes.label: Paper money failure
nodes.full: Facing an empty treasury, the Ilkhan Gaykhatu attempted to introduce Chinese-style paper currency (chao) by decree across Iran — merchants refused to accept it, markets shut down in protest, and the entire experiment collapsed within months, one of history's clearest early demonstrations that currency requires more than a ruler's command to function.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on the failure of the chao currency experiment.

nodes.label: Ghazan conversion and reform
nodes.full: Ghazan Khan's public conversion to Islam in 1295 realigned the Ilkhanate's religious identity with the great majority of its subjects for the first time since the conquest, and his subsequent partnership with the vizier Rashid al-Din produced a sweeping programme of fiscal, administrative and land-tenure reform aimed at repairing the devastation of the conquest era.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on Ghazan's conversion and reforms.

nodes.label: Ghazan converts
nodes.full: Ghazan's public conversion, followed swiftly by his court and much of the Mongol military elite, resolved a religious ambiguity that had defined the Ilkhanate since its founding — a Mongol ruling class now sharing the majority religion of the Iranian population it governed, with real consequences for the state's legitimacy and its subjects' loyalty alike.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, on Ghazan's conversion and its political reception.

nodes.label: Fiscal and land reforms
nodes.full: Ghazan's reform programme standardised tax assessment, restored abandoned agricultural land to cultivation through secure tenure grants, reformed the currency and postal-relay system, and curbed the worst abuses of tax-farming — a deliberate, well-documented attempt to repair seven decades of conquest-era economic damage through targeted state policy.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, describing Ghazan's reform edicts in detail.

nodes.label: Compendium of Chronicles
nodes.full: Commissioned by Ghazan and completed under Oljeitu, Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh compiled histories of the Mongols, Turks, Chinese, Indians, Jews and Franks (western Europeans) into a single work — researched using Mongol, Chinese and even European informants at the cosmopolitan Ilkhanid court — that many historians consider the first genuine world history ever written.
nodes.src: Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Jami al-Tawarikh, illustrated manuscript copies, Edinburgh University Library and elsewhere.

nodes.label: Pax Mongolica
nodes.full: For the first and only time in premodern history, a single political system of allied khanates stretched continuously from Korea to the Black Sea — the Ilkhanate's position at its western end made Iran a genuine crossroads where Chinese, Central Asian, Persian, Arab and, increasingly, European merchants, diplomats and scholars all had reason to pass through or settle.
nodes.src: Comparative Eurasian political geography under the Mongol successor khanates, 13th–14th centuries.

nodes.label: Tabriz trade revival
nodes.full: Unified Mongol control across most of Eurasia, from China to the Black Sea, dramatically reduced the number of separate tolls and tariffs a merchant caravan had to cross — Tabriz grew into one of the greatest trade emporia of the medieval world under these conditions, its markets described in awe by European visitors including Marco Polo's own family.
nodes.src: Marco Polo, The Travels, on Tabriz's commercial importance.

nodes.label: Chinese painting reaches Tabriz
nodes.full: Artists at the Ilkhanid court workshop absorbed Chinese pictorial conventions — cloud bands, dragon and phoenix motifs, landscape composition — carried west along the same trade and diplomatic networks that moved silk, paper technology and astronomical texts, fusing them with Persian manuscript painting to create a genuinely new artistic idiom.
nodes.src: Comparative art-historical analysis of Ilkhanid-period manuscript painting and Yuan-dynasty Chinese painting conventions.

nodes.label: Great Mongol Shahnameh
nodes.full: An extraordinarily lavish illustrated manuscript of Ferdowsi's Persian epic, produced at the Ilkhanid court workshop at Tabriz, fused Chinese painting techniques and motifs — carried east to west along Mongol trade and diplomatic networks — with Persian literary and artistic tradition, founding what art historians call the Ilkhanid school of painting.
nodes.src: Great Mongol Shahnameh (Demotte Shahnameh) folios, dispersed across the Metropolitan Museum, Freer Gallery and other collections.

nodes.label: The Karts of Herat
nodes.full: The Karts, a local dynasty of Ghurid origin, ruled Herat as vassals of the Mongols from 1245: Shams al-Din Muhammad, who succeeded that year, was received by the Great Khan Möngke, who placed Greater Khorasan under his sway, and after subduing Sistan he visited Hulagu in 1263–64. The family kept Herat as an autonomous vassal through the Ilkhanid century and expanded after the Ilkhanate’s fragmentation in 1335, until Timur ended the dynasty in 1381.
nodes.src: Sayf al-Din Harawi, Tarikh-nama-yi Harat, the dynastic chronicle of the Karts; Encyclopaedia Iranica on the Kart dynasty; the Ghurid origin of the family is its own claim and is accepted by many but not all historians.

nodes.label: Negüderi raiders on the Khorasan frontier
nodes.full: From the 1260s roving Mongol bands known as the Negüderis, based in the Afghan highlands, raided Khorasan and exposed Herat to pillage, a recurring insecurity on the Ilkhanate’s eastern march that the vassal Karts and the Ilkhans themselves had to contend with. The raids belong to the wider struggle between the Ilkhanate and the Mongol khanates of Central Asia over the eastern Iranian lands.
nodes.src: Encyclopaedia Iranica on the Kart dynasty and the Negüderis; Rashid al-Din, Jami al-Tawarikh; the chronology of individual raids is imperfectly documented, so the dates given are approximate.

nodes.label: Rumi family leaves Balkh
nodes.full: As the Mongol invasion of Khwarazmia loomed, the preacher Baha al-Din Walad left Balkh around 1216–20 with his family and disciples, travelling west through Baghdad, Mecca, Damascus and Anatolia and settling in Konya around 1229. The journey carried the Khorasani Sufi milieu to Anatolia, where his son Jalal al-Din Rumi became the greatest Persian-language poet of the age; scholars debate whether the invasion itself caused the departure, since the family left before Balkh fell in 1221.
nodes.src: Aflākī, Manāqib al-‘Ārifīn, and Sipahsalar’s biography of Rumi, both later hagiographies; the chronology of the journey and the role of the Mongol threat are reconstructed from these sources and debated.

nodes.label: Oljeitu and Abu Said
nodes.full: Oljeitu built the new capital of Soltaniyeh around his own monumental mausoleum, while his son Abu Sa'id's death in 1335 without a surviving direct heir triggered the Ilkhanate's rapid collapse into rival successor states — the dynasty ending, much like the Seljuks before it, in succession chaos rather than external conquest.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, continuation of Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh, on Abu Sa'id's death and the succession crisis.

nodes.label: Dome of Soltaniyeh
nodes.full: Oljeitu's mausoleum at Soltaniyeh carries one of the largest brick domes ever built, its double-shell structure and turquoise-tiled exterior representing a technical and aesthetic culmination of Persian dome engineering that architectural historians consider a direct influence on later domed structures across the Islamic world.
nodes.src: Soltaniyeh mausoleum, extant structure, UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2005).

nodes.label: Dynasty ends without an heir
nodes.full: Abu Sa'id's sudden death in 1335 without a surviving son to succeed him left the Ilkhanate without any agreed mechanism for choosing a new ruler, and the state fractured within a few years into rival Jalayirid, Muzaffarid, Chobanid and other successor principalities — a collapse triggered entirely from within, not by any external conqueror.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, continuation of Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh, on the succession crisis of 1335.

nodes.label: Khwarazm-Shah kills a Mongol trade mission
nodes.full: The Khwarazm-Shah’s murder of a Mongol trade mission is the provocation Genghis Khan answered with the invasion.
nodes.src: named in this folio’s p1; see the Iran 1055–1219 folio for the Khwarazmian state
